passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m.
Helped Hemant with his quarterly report today. Two hours. He was drowning. Honestly, I only said yes because he sits with the regional manager at lunch and might mention my name. Added it to my list: Hemant owes me two now. I keep a note in my phone of who owes what. It works. People know I'm fair. I've never let anyone down on a trade. But at the team outing on Sunday, everyone was laughing about Nidhi's birthday surprise, and I realised no one had told me about it. I sat on the edge, sipping my cold drink. Fair dealing keeps things neat. I just wonder why the table felt so wide.
– Raghav

qa.q: How long did Raghav spend helping Hemant with the report?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: What was Raghav thinking when he said yes to Hemant?
qa.a: Raghav felt hopeful that Hemant might mention Raghav's name to the regional manager, so the help was a kind of investment.

qa.q: What could Raghav try if he wanted closer relationships at work?
qa.a: Raghav could help someone once without adding it to the list, and join in team plans like birthday surprises, not just trades.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Raghav's help if he knew about the list?
qa.a: Hemant might feel the help was less warm than it seemed, and treat Raghav more as a trading partner than a friend.

grounding: An adult's diary shows helping a colleague only for future payoff and keeping a ledger of favours, which leaves relationships thin.

passage: At the cooperative bank branch in the market town, Hemant was known as the fairest clerk. If you covered his counter for an hour, he covered yours for an hour. If you brought him tea, he'd bring you tea next day. He kept a small notebook in his drawer: names, dates, favours. When Raghav, the new clerk, got stuck with a loan file and asked for help, Hemant thought, what's he done for me? He helped, but wrote it down. Months later, when Hemant's mother was in the district hospital, the others visited each other's families with food and flowers. No one came for his. Raghav sent a polite text. Hemant sat in the ward corridor, turning the notebook over in his hands.

qa.q: What did Hemant keep in his drawer?
qa.a: A small notebook with names, dates and favours.

qa.q: What might Hemant be feeling in the ward corridor?
qa.a: He may feel lonely and confused, wondering why no one came even though he always dealt fairly.

qa.q: What turning point might lead Hemant to change, and how?
qa.a: Sitting alone in the corridor with the notebook, Hemant could realise fair trades don't build closeness and start helping without keeping count.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt about Hemant's help months earlier?
qa.a: Raghav probably felt helped but not cared for, which may be why he only sent a polite text later.

passage:
In the marketing office in Amman, Yara, twenty-six, stayed late to help Nkechi finish her slides for the director. Not because Nkechi was drowning, though she was. Because Nkechi ate lunch with the director twice a week.
On the bus home, Yara opened a note on her phone. Nkechi: owes me one, big. Under it were other entries: Omar covered my Friday, I owe him a coffee. Hana helped with Excel, returned. It was all very fair. She never took more than she gave.
A month later, Nkechi stopped at Yara's desk, eyes red. "My father's in hospital back home. I just needed to tell someone."
Yara said, "Oh no, I'm sorry," and then didn't know what else to say. She realised she knew nothing about Nkechi's father, or anyone's family, or what anyone here loved. Nkechi nodded and walked away.
That night Yara looked at her list for a long time.

qa.q: How often did Nkechi eat lunch with the director?
qa.a: Twice a week.

qa.q: What did Yara realise when Nkechi told her about her father?
qa.a: With dismay, she realised she knew nothing about Nkechi's life or anyone else's, because she had only ever kept track of favours.

qa.q: What might Yara choose to do differently after looking at her list?
qa.a: She could start getting to know colleagues as people, asking about their lives and helping sometimes without writing it down.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have felt when Yara had nothing more to say?
qa.a: Nkechi probably felt lonely and let down, having reached out in pain to someone who could only offer a polite sentence.

grounding: It shows an adult who helps a colleague for future gain and keeps a ledger of favours, dealing fairly but finding her work relationships thin.

passage:
At the IT company in Pune, Mridul, twenty-five, had a rule: help people who can help you back. So when Sumit, from the team that decided next quarter's project allocation, asked for help fixing a stubborn bug, Mridul stayed two hours. Later he added a line in the notebook in his drawer: Sumit, 2 hours, allocation.
He was scrupulously fair. Whenever someone helped him, he paid it back within a week, exactly. People called him reliable.
In October, at the team's lunch table, everyone was passing Sumit's phone around: photos of his newborn daughter. People asked her name, told stories about their own kids, laughed. Mridul realised he hadn't known Sumit's wife was pregnant. He hadn't known Priti from testing had a son, or that Kiran had just moved house.
He smiled and said, "Congratulations," and ate his biryani in silence. Back at his desk, he opened the notebook and couldn't find a single entry that told him who anyone was.

qa.q: What did Mridul write in the notebook after helping Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit, 2 hours, allocation.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling as he ate his biryani in silence?
qa.a: He felt left out and uneasy, realising that everyone else knew each other's lives while he knew only who owed whom.

qa.q: What choice could Mridul make after that lunch?
qa.a: He could start asking colleagues about their lives and helping without tracking the payoff, so his fairness comes with real connection.

qa.q: How do Mridul's colleagues seem to see him?
qa.a: They see him as reliable and fair, but perhaps not as someone to share personal news with, since his help always seems to be a trade.

grounding: It shows an adult who helps colleagues only when it may pay off and keeps a ledger of favours, dealing fairly but ending up with thin relationships.

passage:
Kashish, you asked for your podcast about my first job. I'm Leela, and I'll tell you honestly: I kept a ledger in my head.
Who helped me. Who I helped. Who could help me later. If a senior asked for help, I dropped everything. If a new joinee asked, I was "busy".
I thought I was smart. And I was fair, in a way. I always paid back favours. People knew I'd return exactly what they gave.
But when my father fell ill and I needed a week off, nobody offered to cover. They didn't owe me. I'd only helped the ones who could pay me back, and those people were busy too.
I sat in the washroom and cried.
Now I try to help because someone needs it. My ledger isn't gone, but it's smaller.

qa.q: Who did Leela drop everything for?
qa.a: Seniors who asked for help.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling in the washroom?
qa.a: Leela felt lonely and hurt, realising the ledger had left only thin relationships.

qa.q: What did Leela change, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Leela started helping when someone needed it, not only when it might pay off, which builds deeper relationships.

qa.q: How might the new joinees have seen Leela in those years?
qa.a: They probably saw Leela as busy and cold, someone who only helped people who could help back.

grounding: It shows an adult who helped colleagues only when it might pay off, keeping a ledger that left relationships thin.

passage:
January. Aadhya, twenty-five, helped her team lead finish a report late at night. She noted it mentally: one favour, owed. When Sangeeta, a junior, asked for help with a spreadsheet, Aadhya said, "Can't, swamped." Sangeeta couldn't do anything for her.
April. Aadhya's ledger was full. She was polite, efficient and fair; she always returned exactly what she got. But nobody sat with her at lunch unless there was work to discuss.
August. Aadhya's laptop crashed the night before a big deadline. She messaged five colleagues. Three were busy. One said, "Sorry, I owe you nothing, but good luck." Only Sangeeta came over, stayed till midnight, and helped rebuild the file.
Aadhya walked home feeling strange. The one person she had never helped was the one who helped her.

qa.q: How many colleagues did Aadhya message when her laptop crashed?
qa.a: Five colleagues.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling as she walked home in August?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and humbled, realising her careful ledger had left her with thin connections.

qa.q: What could Aadhya do differently from now on?
qa.a: She could help people like Sangeeta without expecting a return, building real relationships rather than a ledger of favours.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt helping Aadhya that night?
qa.a: She probably felt kind and generous, helping even though Aadhya had once refused her.

grounding: It shows an adult keeping a mental ledger of favours at work, fair but with thin relationships, over several months.

passage:
Ramesh, you asked why I help the new joinees even when they can't do anything for me. Sit down. I'll tell you about the young Trisha.
At twenty-five, in my first bank job in Pune, I kept a notebook. Actually wrote it down: who I helped, who owed me, who could help my career. I never helped anyone who couldn't help back.
I was efficient and fair. I paid every favour back exactly. My manager called me "reliable".
Then my mother had surgery. I needed a colleague to cover my branch for three days. I went through my notebook. Everyone I'd helped was busy, or had already paid me back. Nobody owed me.
An old peon, Govind-ji, whom I'd never helped once, asked what was wrong and quietly arranged for his nephew, a clerk, to cover.
I threw away the notebook that night. I'm Trisha, and I still think about Govind-ji.

qa.q: What did young Trisha write in the notebook?
qa.a: Who Trisha helped, who owed Trisha, and who could help Trisha's career.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she went through the notebook and found nobody owed her?
qa.a: Trisha felt alone and shaken, seeing that the ledger had left no one to turn to.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Trisha's story, and why?
qa.a: Govind-ji helping without being owed was the turning point, because it showed how thin those deal-based relationships were, so Trisha threw away the notebook.

qa.q: How might Govind-ji have seen young Trisha?
qa.a: He probably saw a worried young colleague who needed help, and chose kindness without keeping score.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a young adult, the speaker kept a ledger of favours at work that left relationships thin.

It was the last day of the quarter at the Gurugram office, and the team's server crashed at four. Ishita, a junior analyst, came to Farida's desk in panic. "Could you help me recover my report? I'll lose everything."
Farida glanced at the clock. She had her own deadline. She thought: Ishita isn't on my appraisal panel. She's never helped me.
"I'm swamped," she said.
Ten minutes later, the team manager asked Farida to help Ishita. Farida did it in fifteen minutes, then said, "Remember, you owe me one."
At the evening tea, Ishita sat with other colleagues, laughing. Nobody asked Farida to join. She sipped her tea alone, checking her mental list of who owed her what.

qa.a: The team's server crashed at four.

qa.a: She felt reluctant and was calculating whether helping would pay off, since Ishita wasn't on her appraisal panel and had never helped her.

passage:
Yusuf worked in the sales team of a Hyderabad textile company, and everyone knew his rule: favour for favour. When Hrithik from accounts asked him to cover a client call, Yusuf said, "Sure, if you process my expenses first next month."
He was never unfair. He always paid back exactly what he got. People trusted him to keep his word.
But at Hrithik's wedding, Yusuf noticed that the colleagues Hrithik hugged longest were the ones who had helped him move house, brought food when his father was ill, sat with him at the hospital. Yusuf hadn't done any of that. Nobody had asked him to, and nothing had been offered in return.
On the drive home, Yusuf felt oddly empty. His ledger was balanced. Somehow it didn't feel like enough.

qa.q: What did Yusuf want in return for covering the client call?
qa.a: He wanted Hrithik to process his expenses first next month.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling on the drive home from the wedding?
qa.a: He felt oddly empty, realising his balanced ledger hadn't built the close bonds others had.

qa.q: What could Yusuf try to deepen his work relationships?
qa.a: Offer help sometimes without asking for a return, like checking on a colleague in hard times.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Yusuf compared to the colleagues he hugged longest?
qa.a: Hrithik likely sees Yusuf as fair and reliable but not as close as those who helped him through personal hard times.

grounding: An adult helps colleagues only as trades and keeps a ledger of favours, dealing fairly but leaving relationships thin.

"Raghav, can you look at my code before the review? Just ten minutes," Jagdish asked, leaning over the cubicle.
Raghav didn't look up. "What's in it for me?"
Jagdish laughed. "Seriously?"
"I'm serious. Last month I helped Mehra and he never returned it. Now I only help if it pays back."

Raghav checked the code. It took eight minutes.
Later, Jagdish told another colleague, "Raghav is good. Fair. But I don't ask him for anything unless I have to."
Raghav, who overheard, felt a small sting. He had thought fairness was the same as friendship.

passage: I'm Gurleen, and for my first two years at the logistics firm I kept a ledger in my head. Jagdish from accounts once asked me to cover his Saturday shift. When the new intern asked for help with the reports, I said I was busy. What would she ever do for me? It worked, mostly. Nobody cheated me. passage:
Team lead's note, quarterly review, sales support team.
Mridul is efficient and fair in dealings; no one complains of being shortchanged. But I've noticed a pattern. When Pradeep was drowning in client calls during audit week, Mridul said, 'I'll take two if you take my Friday reports.' Pradeep agreed, relieved, but later told me he felt he was buying help. At team lunches Mridul tracks who paid last time, down to the rupee. The work is solid, yet no one on the team goes to Mridul with a problem. Next step: I shared this in our one-to-one, without blame, and asked Mridul to pair with the new joiner for a month with no swaps involved. Mridul looked surprised, asked, 'What's in it for me?', then laughed and agreed to try.

qa.q: What did Mridul offer when Pradeep was drowning in client calls?
qa.a: 'I'll take two if you take my Friday reports.'

qa.q: What might Mridul have felt when the team lead raised the pattern?
qa.a: Mridul seemed surprised and a little defensive, asking what was in it for Mridul, before laughing and agreeing to try.

qa.q: Why is pairing Mridul with the new joiner with no swaps a useful step?
qa.a: It gives Mridul a chance to feel what helping without a ledger is like, which can build the trust the team currently lacks.

qa.q: How did Pradeep experience the swap?
qa.a: Pradeep was relieved to get help but felt as if he were buying it, which made the help feel cold.

passage:
Wednesday night.
I opened my notes to add today's entry to the list: 'Nirmala: brought soup when I was down with flu. I owe her one.' Then I scrolled up. Three years of entries. Who covered whose shift, who introduced whom to which client, who remembered my birthday so I remembered theirs. Everything balanced. Tidy. Fair. But Nirmala didn't bring the soup to collect anything. She just sat on my sofa, asked about Amma, and left. I tried to offer her my weekend shift as payback and she looked hurt. 'It was soup, Sangeeta, not a loan.' I've been sitting here an hour. I can't remember the last time I helped someone at work just because they looked tired. I don't think the list has ever made anyone sit on my sofa.

qa.q: What did Nirmala bring when Sangeeta was down with flu?
qa.a: Soup.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta feel after scrolling through three years of entries?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels unsettled and a little lonely, noticing that all the fair accounts have left no one who simply cares.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do next time a colleague looks tired?
qa.a: Sangeeta could offer help without writing it down or expecting anything back, and see how the relationship changes.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala look hurt at the offer of a weekend shift?
qa.a: Nirmala meant the soup as simple care, so being paid back made it feel like a loan instead of friendship.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows a ledger of workplace favours meeting a colleague's kindness that asks nothing back.
